lastText: File ClosedDestroyed in PlaceMajor DefeatWehrmacht High Command, 1939–1945End of hostilities: JANUARY 1945 (PROJECTED) · filed with minor delayImmediate AftermathThe end comes early, around January 1945: the calendar itself the clearest casualty of this path's decisions. What surrenders at the end is less an army than a casualty ledger with a rear echelon. And it ended immobile: whatever strength remained stood where it stood, out of fuel, defending only what it could walk to. So little organized force remained by the end that both Allied advances accelerated freely: the final meeting line lands wherever logistics, not resistance, decided. Sea Lion was actually launched, the September crossing every staff study warned against, and the army fought the rest of the war missing the assault divisions it left on English shingle. Sixth Army left the Volga as an army: the single largest body of men any decision in this campaign moves from the dead column to the living. One thread runs the full length of this campaign back to May 1940: pressing the attack at Dunkirk thinned the veteran leadership Britain historically rebuilt around: a quiet effect, still present in the British sector a dozen decisions later. The Bismarck never sailed: held in port rather than risked on the Atlantic breakout that historically cost the Royal Navy the Hood and cost the Kriegsmarine the ship itself within a week. Every road in this campaign bends the same way in the end: toward defeat, not around it. What
